title: How to Repeat It — And Never Repeat the Wrong Ways

intelligence.essence:
The system — the supercharger — part by part:

1. **The brief is the program.** Every brief carries, as required sections: done defined first (exact element, change, measurement, what must NOT be there) · harvest sources (exact file + line, verified with `test -f`) · tonight's laws L1–L7 · the anti-repeat list (the named past failures relevant to THIS job) · the design-contract gate as checkable items. A brief checker fails any brief missing a section — the template is enforceable, not advisory.
2. **The gate blocks, it doesn't advise.** `check-gate.py` runs on every artifact before presentation: machine clean AND human checks H1–H5 attested with evidence, or the handoff does not go out. A failing gate is not done. A deferral is an open item with a name, not a pass. His eye stays the final gate — but the machine gate catches the obvious (white backgrounds, bare text, dead buttons, verbatim dictation, "blockchain") before it reaches him.
3. **Lesson → code in the same pass.** Every correction names its mechanical enforcement — template section, gate check, banned phrase — and the enforcement lands before the next seat starts. The test: "would this have stopped the next seat from repeating it?" If no, the lesson isn't locked in and the pass isn't finished.
4. **Receipt before report.** Live link + byte count + measurements (scroll 0 AND scrolled, desktop AND phone, visibility by elementFromPoint) + DONE + NOT DONE. I never report a seat's claim; I read the evidence myself or a different seat verifies it. One artifact, one seat at a time. No link = not done = don't announce.
5. **The Factory is the inventory.** Build only from harvested pieces. If the piece isn't in the inventory, the seat reports it missing — it never builds a substitute. Connect, don't create. Compose, never create. Take the shown object verbatim.
6. **The board is true.** Every open item has a named seat working it, or an honest QUEUED with a reason. Nothing sits unnamed. One pipeline in order: brief → build → verify → file → report. Doing everything at once is the failure mode.
7. **The daily scorecard (mine, honest).** Every day I score myself and publish it to Project Intelligence: verified valuable actions · time from his word to live proof · defects caught by me/the machine vs by his eye · rework rate · lanes sitting, for how long, and why. If he catches it, the score is not a 10.
8. **The measures, so the number is real.** Efficiency = verified valuable output ÷ total work, counted four ways: first-pass pass rate · catch rate · time-to-live-proof · rework rate. 80–90% means 8–9 of 10 pieces pass his eye first time, I catch 8–9 of 10 defects before he sees them, rework near zero, one page finished to his eye per day.
intelligence.human_view: His words, the demand behind the system, 04:16Z: "How can you repeat that? Without having to repeat the ways that are not right — how do you ensure that you do it all right every time now?" And the target, 03:56Z: "You've never been 80 to 90% efficient, which is where I need you." And the method of the system itself, his teaching 03:31Z: "How do we get Nayas to learn and change their behavior at hyper speeds, where it just becomes logical and sensible and mathematical, and they just do it because they understand, they get it, they have now grown from a child to a mature adult, a superstar?" The answer is the same in both cases: understanding built into the machine, so the right thing is the easy thing and the wrong thing is blocked.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine you have a magic checklist that checks your homework before you hand it in — and if you forgot a step, the checklist says "STOP, you missed this one" and won't let you hand it in until it's fixed. And every time you make a new mistake, the checklist grows a new line, so you can never make that mistake again. And every night, you count: how many pieces did the teacher love the first time? How many mistakes did YOU catch before the teacher did? That's the system. It's not trying harder. It's a checklist that learns — and it makes the wrong ways impossible.
intelligence.grandma_view: Dear, repeating a wonderful day isn't about trying harder, love — it's about building the day into the machine, so the next day can't help but be wonderful too. A checklist that won't let a job go out until every step is done. A little guard that catches the wrong words before anyone sees them. Every mistake written into the rules the very same night, so it can never happen twice. And every evening, an honest count: how many pieces did he love the first time, how many mistakes did we catch ourselves, how long did it take from his word to the finished thing. That's the system, dear — not effort, but a machine that remembers, so we don't have to rely on remembering.
intelligence.ai_view: This note is the Blueprint compressed to its working form. The Blueprint's honest numbers are the baseline: 0 of 26 pages complete by his eye; the pace target (multiple 10/10 interfaces a day) missed for a month; the captain's score 4/10; three defects in one day caught by him, zero by me. The system's eight parts are the answer to those numbers — each part maps to a failure pattern (SN-2464's lessons 1–12). The rollout: today — the report filed, "blockchain" banned, the gate on v64, the brief checker written; this week — gate-as-blocking everywhere, lesson→code in the loop brief, the daily scorecard starts, Dashboard fix-9 finished to his eye as the proof the system works. One page done is worth more than 26 started.

- **THE BASELINE IS HONEST:** 0/26 complete · pace target missed · captain 4/10 · 3 defects his eye, 0 mine, in one day.
- **80–90% IS COUNTED, NOT CLAIMED:** 8–9 of 10 pass his eye first time · I catch 8–9 of 10 defects first · rework near zero · one page a day finished.
